extracted.intended_audience: e-text transcribers / digital editors preparing plain-ASCII editions (Project Gutenberg-style)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for preparing a plain-ASCII e-text edition of an early modern printed work (here, Hobbes' Leviathan), covering decisions about capitalization, italics, margin notes, foreign alphabets, references, and preservation of original spelling/punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow original edition closely with unavoidable differences
rubrics_metrics.description: This E-text was prepared from the Pelican Classics edition of Leviathan, which in turn was prepared from the first edition. I have tried to follow as closely as possible the original, and to give the flavour of the text that Hobbes himself proof-read, but the following differences were unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to reproduce the original typography and text where feasible, but accept and document necessary departures in a transcriber's note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve Hobbes' extensive use of capitals and italics
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes used capitals and italics very extensively, for emphasis, for proper names, for quotations, and sometimes, it seems, just because.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt to reflect Hobbes' use of capitals and italics in the e-text so the flavour and emphases of the original remain apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict full capitalization to original occurrences; uniformize chapter headings
rubrics_metrics.description: I have restricted my use of full capitalization to those places where Hobbes used it, except in the chapter headings, which I have fully capitalized, where Hobbes used a mixture of full capitalization and italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply blanket full-capital formatting; preserve original full-capital instances. For chapter headings where the original mixed styles, render them fully capitalized for clarity/consistency in plain text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render italics used for quotations by adding quotation marks and retaining original capitalization inside quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it is clear that the italics are to indicate the text is quoting, I have introduced quotation marks. Within quotation marks I have retained the capitalization that Hobbes used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When italics function as quotation in the original, mark quotations with standard ASCII quotation marks and keep any original capitalization inside the quote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent italics used for emphasis or proper names by capitalizing initial letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Where italics seem to be used for emphasis, or for proper names, or just because, I have capitalized the initial letter of the words. This has the disadvantage that they are not then distinguished from those that Hobbes capitalized in plain text, but the extent of his italics would make the text very ugly if I was to use an underscore or slash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In plain-ASCII transcriptions, prefer initial-capitalization for words originally italicized for emphasis/proper names, rather than adding intrusive markup like underscores or slashes; note the trade-off (loss of distinction from normal capitals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include margin notes as paragraph headers with initial capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the margin notes are either to introduce the paragraph subject, or to show where he introduces word definitions, I have included them as headers to the paragraph, again with all words having initial capitals, and on a shortened line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat marginalia that function as topical markers or definitions as short header lines preceding the paragraph; render them with initial capitals and on a shortened line to simulate margin-note function in linear text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place margin references to quotations inline in brackets immediately after the quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: For margin references to quotes, I have included them in the text, in brackets immediately next to the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When marginal references refer to quotations, insert them inline in round (or bracketed) form immediately after the quoted passage so the reference remains associated with the quote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert square brackets in main text references to round brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Hobbes included references in the main text, I have left them as he put them, except to change his square brackets to round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalize bracket style for readability in plain text by converting square brackets used by the original author in main text references into round parentheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute Greek alphabet with nearest ordinary letters and capitalize foreign words' initials
rubrics_metrics.description: For the Greek alphabet, I have simply substituted the nearest ordinary letters that I can, and I have used initial capitals for foreign language words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When original uses non-Latin scripts (Greek), transliterate into nearest ASCII letters; mark foreign-language words by capitalizing their initial letter to indicate they are foreign terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduce original spelling and punctuation where possible (except added quotation marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither Thomas Hobbes nor his typesetters seem to have had many inhibitions about spelling and punctuation. I have tried to reproduce both exactly, with the exception of the introduction of quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve historical spelling and punctuation faithfully in the transcription to retain original character and meaning, only modernizing or adding minimal markers (e.g., quotation marks) when necessary for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reading aloud/subvocalization to interpret emphasis and eccentric punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: In preparing the text, I have found that it has much more meaning if I read it with sub-vocalization, or aloud, rather than trying to read silently. Hobbes’ use of emphasis and his eccentric punctuation and construction seem then to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/transcribers should consider reading passages aloud or subvocalizing to capture intended emphases and to inform faithful representation of punctuation/intonation in the plain-text edition.
